newsitem.title: FRANCE: Troops patrol France after suspected Algerian bomb.
newsitem.headline: Troops patrol France after suspected Algerian bomb.

text.p: Troops patrolled French cities and borders on Thursday in response to Tuesday's bomb in a Paris rush-hour train by suspected Algerian Islamic guerrillas which killed two people and triggered fears of new rash of attacks.

Police appealed to travellers who used the suburban railway line around the time of the blast to get in touch, and set up a freephone number after questioning dozens of witnesses without apparently getting strong leads.

Interior Minister Jean-Louis Debre pointed to "extremely worrying similarities" between the attack and a spate of bombs last year claimed by Moslem rebels fighting Algeria's French-backed military government.
"There are similarities not only in the make-up of the device but also in the methods used," he told Radio Luxembourg.

In a high-profile show of strength designed to reassure and deter, soldiers and police guarded railway stations in Paris and major cities, and tightened surveillance at borders, airports and tourist sites like the Eiffel Tower. A total of 1,800 troops were ordered out to back up police, including 800 in Paris.

Spot checks were made on cars on the Champs-Elysees avenue and guards at stores searched Christmas shoppers' bags. Police handed stickers to travellers on the Metro underground railway urging them to watch out for suspect packages.
Trains resumed on the RER suburban line where the bomb exploded in Tuesday's evening rush-hour at Port Royal station.

Twenty-two people were still in hospital on Thursday after the blast, which killed two people and injured 91. The dead were a Canadian woman, Helene Viel, and a Frenchman from New Caledonia, Lucien Devambez.

Prime Minister Alain Juppe met Debre for a briefing on the the so-called Vigipirate plan, reimposed after the 1995 bombs claimed by the radical Algerian Armed Islamic Group (GIA) that killed eight people and wounded more than 160 others.
Debre said France had been at "constant risk" since last year and that investigators had kept up probes and arrests. "There are today almost 200 Islamists in prison," he said.
He dismissed press suggestions that France had had clear warnings of imminent attacks.

Investigators focused on Algerian militants, battling the French-backed military government in a war that has claimed an estimated 50,000 lives since 1992 when Algiers scrapped elections that Islamic fundamentalists were poised to win.
The daily Le Monde said the bombers used an electronic timer from a cooker as a detonator, slightly more sophisticated than the alarm clocks with metal hands used in last year's bombs.
In other ways, the bomb was identical to the 1995 devices, stuffed into a hollowed-out gas canister with nails.
The daily Liberation said French secret services had been worried by threats by the new leader of the GIA, Antar Zouabri.
"France fights Moslems. That's why we maintain the same attitude towards this country as our predecessors, the emirs of the GIA," it quoted Zouabri as saying in September.

The conservative daily Le Figaro headlined its edition "Terrorism: the Tarek trail", referring to the codename of Ali Touchent, a 39-year-old architect suspected of organising last year's bombings who escaped a huge security crackdown.
Municipal workers continued sealing off thousands of rubbish bins around the capital and installing 14,000 crash barriers to prevent car bombs from being parked near school entrances.
Police banned school outings from the Metro, ordered public toilets locked and stepped up surveillance at street markets -- all targets of bomb attacks in 1995 in Paris and Lyon.
